evidence: The 1989 USP thesis O nascimento da economia política no Brasil precedes the 1996 book on Cairu and political economy in slaveholding Brazil. Rocha’s 1989 USP article explicitly identifies that thesis as his research.

Editora Unesp identifies the author of Abolicionistas brasileiros e ingleses and A economia política na sociedade escravista as a professor in USP’s History Department, matching the USP supervisor anchor; USP also records him supervising a 2002 economic-history doctorate.
The 2007 thesis and 2009 book have the same distinctive title, Gente negra na Paraíba oitocentista: população, família e parentesco espiritual, fitting direct thesis-to-book development.

Cambridge’s author biography for Indian Affairs and the Administrative State identifies Stephen J. Rockwell as a professor at St. Joseph’s College, matching the reviewer’s institution, and credits American Government: Competition and Compromise as well.

Carmem Izabel’s books concern urban anthropology, sociability and identities in Belém; her related doctorate was at UFPE in 2006. Carmem Marques’s 2022 UFMG history thesis concerns eighteenth-century cartographers and the 1807 map Colombia Prima, a separate career and full name.

De costa a costa (2005) studies sailors, slave-trade intermediaries and Angola–Brazil maritime connections in 1780–1860; the ORCID works continue that specific research on Portuguese and Luso-Brazilian merchant crews, shipboard conflict and sailors’ social history in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

João Paulo Coelho de Souza Rodrigues wrote the 2001 book on literature and politics in the Brazilian Academy of Letters and earned his doctorate at Unicamp in 2002. João Lucas Rodrigues’s 2023 UFMG thesis studies coffee, land and labor in southwestern Minas Gerais; the full names and academic careers differ.

Colonial Routes (2010 thesis) and Amazonian Routes (2014 book) both specifically study spatial mobility and community formation in the colonial Portuguese Amazon, with a plausible thesis-to-book interval.

Both work lists include The sea! The sea! (2005/2006); the ORCID publications on Thucydides, Xenophon’s Anabasis and its modern reception continue the books’ distinctive classical historiography and reception research.
The 1967 thesis on the functioning of French ambassadors under Louis XIV directly anticipates The age of Louis XIV: the rise of modern diplomacy (1976), followed by another book on diplomacy in 1986.

The 1972 thesis examines Mexicano resistance to Anglo-American control in New Mexico, 1870–1900; Mexicano resistance in the Southwest (1981) develops the same specific subject, alongside the 1980 survey of Mexican Americans in Texas.

The 2005 thesis Re-Imaging Indian Country concerns American Indians in metropolitan Los Angeles; the 2012 book Reimagining Indian country studies Native migration and identity in twentieth-century Los Angeles, a direct thesis-to-book connection.

Penn identifies the author of the Julio-Claudian, Gordion and Troy books as an archaeologist with a 1987 Columbia PhD and 1978 BA. He cannot be the author of the 1971 thesis The Evolution of the Image of Venice (1500–1630).

Markets and Massachusetts Farmers (1984 thesis), on rural New England’s economic growth in 1750–1855, directly anticipates From market-places to a market economy (1992), on rural Massachusetts’s transformation in 1750–1850.

The ORCID works on Byzantine enslavement, manumission and slavery continue the specific subject of the 2004 and 2009 books. Tel Aviv University lists both books under Youval Rotman and describes his research on slavery and social abnormality, also explaining the psychology-related articles.
